hints: Focus on counting all the valence electrons around carbon, remembering that a charge adds or removes electrons.
Carbon brings 4 valence electrons and each H contributes 1, so start from 7 electrons and then adjust for the + or - charge.
Look for the species that has two electrons left over after forming three C-H bonds, as those two form the lone pair.
walkthrough:
**Count valence electrons simply**

Think of this as book-keeping for electrons. Carbon always brings 4 valence electrons and each hydrogen brings 1.

Rule:
$$\text{total valence} = 4 + (1 \times \text{number of H}) - \text{charge}$$

**Apply to the four species**

For $\text{CH}_3$ the total is $4 + 3 = 7$. For $\text{CH}_3^+$ it is $7 - 1 = 6$. For $\text{CH}_3^-$ it is $7 + 1 = 8$. For $\text{CH}_4$ it is $4 + 4 = 8$.

Now subtract 2 electrons for each C-H bond.

**Spot the lone pair**

Only $\text{CH}_3^-$ has 8 electrons with just 3 bonds. That uses 6 electrons in bonding and leaves 2 as a non-bonding lone pair on carbon.

options.A: Incorrect. $\text{CH}_3$ is the methyl radical with 7 valence electrons. Three bonds use 6 electrons, leaving one single unpaired electron, not a paired lone pair.
options.B: Incorrect. $\text{CH}_3^+$ has lost one electron, so only 6 valence electrons remain. All 6 are used in the three C-H bonds, leaving an empty p orbital and no lone pair.
options.C: Correct. $\text{CH}_3^-$ has 8 valence electrons. Three C-H bonds use 6 electrons, leaving 2 electrons as a lone pair on carbon, similar to ammonia.
options.D: Incorrect. $\text{CH}_4$ has 8 valence electrons but forms four C-H bonds. All 8 electrons are bonding, so there is no lone pair left on carbon.
